A. A local research group in Alderford investigated urban trees. Earlier proposals had concentrated on buying equipment, but the new study asked whether tree planting could improve everyday outcomes. The proposed explanation was that canopy cover blocks sunlight before it reaches the pavement. The researchers described this mechanism as shade, while stressing that a plausible explanation alone is not evidence of success.

B. The evaluation in Alderford used a matched comparison group. The team included 8 sites and collected information from 120 participants. Baseline monitoring began in 2012, before the programme was introduced. The intervention phase lasted 6 months. Researchers measured temperatures at midday; all measurements followed the same written procedure. A separate team checked the records without being told which sites had received the intervention first.

C. On a standardised index of surface temperatures, where a lower score represented a better outcome, the average fell from 80 to 72. The authors did not interpret this change as proof that the programme would work everywhere. They noted that seasonal changes can alter the amount of shade. They also cautioned that a short evaluation may miss effects that emerge only over several years.

D. The report recommended a longer follow-up before extending the programme. It did not include a calculation of financial savings, and participation was voluntary. The next phase would examine whether the observed change could be sustained when the research team was no longer present. Local officials agreed to publish the methods so that other teams could repeat the work.

Earlier proposals had concentrated on buying equipment, but the new study asked whether automatic camera surveys could improve everyday outcomes. The proposed explanation was that automatic equipment records activity when observers are absent. The researchers described this mechanism as coverage, while stressing that a plausible explanation alone is not evidence of success.

B. The evaluation in Alderford used a random allocation of sites. The team included 24 sites and collected information from 228 participants. Baseline monitoring began in 2014, before the programme was introduced. The intervention phase lasted 11 months. Researchers compared camera records with manual surveys; all measurements followed the same written procedure. A separate team checked the records without being told which sites had received the intervention first.

C. On a standardised index of missed observations, where a lower score represented a better outcome, the average fell from 83 to 74. The authors did not interpret this change as proof that the programme would work everywhere. They noted that equipment can fail during prolonged wet weather. They also cautioned that a short evaluation may miss effects that emerge only over several years.

D. The report recommended a longer follow-up before extending the programme. It did not include a calculation of financial savings, and participation was voluntary. The next phase would examine whether the observed change could be sustained when the research team was no longer present. Local officials agreed to publish the methods so that other teams could repeat the work.

Earlier proposals had concentrated on buying equipment, but the new study asked whether protected cycle lanes could improve everyday outcomes. The proposed explanation was that physical barriers separate cyclists from moving vehicles. The researchers described this mechanism as separation, while stressing that a plausible explanation alone is not evidence of success.

B. The evaluation in Glenford used a retrospective comparison. The team included 13 sites and collected information from 222 participants. Baseline monitoring began in 2021, before the programme was introduced. The intervention phase lasted 8 months. Researchers reviewed video recordings of junctions; all measurements followed the same written procedure. A separate team checked the records without being told which sites had received the intervention first.

C. On a standardised index of conflicts at junctions, where a lower score represented a better outcome, the average fell from 95 to 80. The authors did not interpret this change as proof that the programme would work everywhere. They noted that junction design can remain a source of risk. They also cautioned that a short evaluation may miss effects that emerge only over several years.

D. The report recommended a longer follow-up before extending the programme. It did not include a calculation of financial savings, and participation was voluntary. The next phase would examine whether the observed change could be sustained when the research team was no longer present. Local officials agreed to publish the methods so that other teams could repeat the work.

Receptionist: Welcome to the Alderford learning centre. Are you asking about our community gardening course?
Visitor: Yes. The leaflet says it is on Wednesday.
Receptionist: That was the original arrangement. It has moved to Monday, although the starting time is still 9:15. Please arrive fifteen minutes early for registration.
Visitor: Is it still in room 30?
Receptionist: No, we are using room 20 now. The larger room is being repaired. The fee is 25 pounds for the whole course, or 20 pounds if you are a student. Materials are included.
Visitor: How long does it run, and is there space available?
Receptionist: It lasts 4 weeks. We can accept up to 12 participants. You need to book by Saturday. Please bring a notebook; everything else is provided. Payment can be made by card, but the booking itself must be completed online.
Visitor: How do I find the room?
Receptionist: From the main entrance, pass the reception desk, turn left at the stairs, and continue to the end of the corridor. The room is opposite the café. The entrance beside the car park is closed.
Tutor: We are also evaluating this course. Our main aim is to compare two teaching methods. We considered interviewing only the most confident participants, but that would give a distorted picture. Instead, we will invite everyone to complete an anonymous questionnaire. Taking part in the evaluation is optional and will not affect anyone's place on the course. We will report the results as group averages, without naming individuals.

passages.dd2d6c34021625bd:
A. A council considering a repair voucher initially assumed that price was the main reason residents discarded appliances. Its survey seemed to support this view: respondents repeatedly called repair expensive. Yet interviews revealed that the word covered several different concerns. Some residents meant the technician's fee; others meant taking a day off work, transporting a heavy item, or paying for a diagnosis without knowing whether a repair would follow. A reduction in the advertised price would address only the first of these concerns.

B. The council therefore tested two offers. One group received a discount on the repair itself; another received a free initial diagnosis and a written estimate, but paid the full price if they proceeded. More people in the second group booked an inspection. This did not mean that more appliances were ultimately repaired: some estimates showed that replacement would be cheaper. The evaluation separated inspection bookings from completed repairs, rather than treating both as evidence of success.

C. Manufacturers argued that products with sealed components were cheaper to assemble and more resistant to moisture. Repairers accepted that these advantages could be real, but pointed out that a minor fault might then require replacement of an entire module. The disagreement was not simply between durable and fragile products. A design could prevent one kind of failure while making another more costly to fix. Counting years of use alone would conceal this difference.

D. The proposed policy consequently combined clearer estimates with requirements to supply spare parts. It stopped short of promising that every item should be repaired. An old appliance might consume substantially more electricity than a replacement; an infrequently used one might not. The council recommended comparing the additional resources required to manufacture a new product with the resources saved during its expected use. Without such a comparison, either a universal repair rule or a universal replacement rule could be environmentally misleading.
passages.21d4690cce4f502e:
A. A city extended its night bus timetable after a survey of hospital and hospitality workers. The survey asked when shifts ended, and planners scheduled departures shortly afterwards. Passenger numbers nevertheless remained below the forecast. It was tempting to conclude that employees preferred driving, but follow-up interviews exposed a problem with the original question: a scheduled shift ending did not always indicate when a person could actually leave the building.

B. Some hospital employees had to wait for a replacement colleague; restaurant workers often finished cleaning after customers had left. A bus timed precisely to the published end of a shift could therefore be missed even on an ordinary evening. The next departure was an hour later. For workers whose finishing times varied, reliability meant being able to get home within a tolerable interval, rather than having a vehicle arrive punctually at a single advertised minute.

C. The transport authority considered running smaller vehicles more frequently. This would reduce waiting but increase the number of drivers required. A contractor proposed an on-demand service instead. Its simulation suggested that vehicles could collect several workers whose journeys overlapped. However, the simulation assumed that requests were known twenty minutes before departure. The hospital could not guarantee that notice, so the predicted efficiency depended on an assumption that was doubtful for a major user group.

D. A trial combined fixed departures with a limited number of additional trips requested at short notice. Researchers reported both average waiting time and the longest waits experienced by a small proportion of passengers. The average alone looked favourable, but concealed evenings when several unexpected requests arrived together. The final report did not reject the hybrid service. It recommended reserving capacity for unusually busy periods and assessing whether the improvement for the worst-served passengers justified the additional staffing cost.

questions.q: What did the interviews reveal about the survey responses?
options: Residents were referring to several kinds of cost.
Most residents had misunderstood what an appliance was.
The technician’s fee was unimportant to every respondent.
Residents were primarily concerned about electricity tariffs.
questions.why: A 段将 expensive 分解为维修费、误工、运输和诊断不确定性，不能将其理解为单一价格问题。
questions.topic: Repair and the price of convenience

questions.q: Why did the evaluation distinguish bookings from completed repairs?
options: The council had stopped collecting booking figures.
Every inspection had to be followed by a replacement.
The two groups received identical financial offers.
An inspection could lead to a decision not to repair.
questions.why: B 段指出有些估价显示换新更便宜，预约检查增长不等于实际维修增长。
questions.topic: Repair and the price of convenience

questions.q: Which heading best captures paragraph C?
options: A disagreement about the cost of spare parts alone
The disappearance of professional repair services
A design trade-off that simple durability measures miss
Proof that sealed products always last longer
questions.why: C 段讨论密封设计防潮的好处与整模块更换成本之间的权衡。
questions.topic: Repair and the price of convenience

questions.q: The group offered a free diagnosis completed more repairs than the discount group.
questions.why: B 段只确认预约更多，并明确提醒不能由此推出维修更多；未提供两组最终维修数。
questions.topic: Repair and the price of convenience

questions.q: The repairers denied that sealed components could provide any practical benefit.
questions.why: C 段明确说维修者承认这些好处可能真实存在，与 denied any benefit 矛盾。
questions.topic: Repair and the price of convenience

questions.q: What is the author’s main reservation about a policy of always repairing appliances?
options: It would make all appliances less resistant to moisture.
It assumes that inspections are more expensive than repairs.
Environmental outcomes depend on production and subsequent use.
questions.why: D 段要求同时比较制造新产品的资源投入与使用阶段节省；结论依赖具体条件。
questions.topic: Repair and the price of convenience

questions.q: What was the main weakness of the original survey?
options: It treated scheduled shift endings as actual departure times.
It included workers who never travelled at night.
It asked workers about travel costs instead of schedules.
It assumed that all workers owned cars.
questions.why: A、B 段共同说明计划下班时间不等于真正离开工作场所的时间。
questions.topic: When a bus timetable is not enough

questions.q: For the workers described in paragraph B, what mattered most about reliability?
options: Having every journey made by the same driver
Arriving at work before the published shift start
Being able to reserve a specific seat
Avoiding an excessive wait despite variable finishing times
questions.why: B 段把 reliability 重新定义为可接受等待区间，不只是某一班车准点。
questions.topic: When a bus timetable is not enough

questions.q: Why might the contractor’s efficiency estimate be too optimistic?
options: It assumed that smaller vehicles required more fuel.
It counted only journeys beginning at restaurants.
It relied on advance notice that some workers could not provide.
It excluded the possibility of sharing vehicles.
questions.why: C 段模拟假设提前二十分钟知道需求，但医院无法保证，削弱模拟适用性。
questions.topic: When a bus timetable is not enough

questions.q: The proposed smaller vehicles would require fewer drivers than the existing service.
questions.why: C 段明确指出更频繁发车会增加所需司机数量。
questions.topic: When a bus timetable is not enough

questions.q: Which measure revealed a problem that the average waiting time obscured?
options: The longest waits experienced by a minority of passengers
The total number of restaurants in the city
The average age of the vehicle fleet
The proportion of drivers working full-time
questions.why: D 段将平均等待与少部分人的极长等待对比，后者暴露高峰需求问题。
questions.topic: When a bus timetable is not enough

questions.q: Which statement best represents the report’s final position?
options: Every fixed departure should immediately be removed.
Low initial ridership proves that night transport is unnecessary.
Average waiting time should be the sole criterion of success.
The hybrid approach merits refinement and a cost-benefit assessment.
questions.why: D 段没有否定混合方案，而是建议预留容量并评估改善与额外成本是否相称。
questions.topic: When a bus timetable is not enough
